summary: Describes a robust method for Path MTU Discovery in which TCP or another packetization layer probes an Internet path with progressively larger packets. It extends RFC 1191 and RFC 1981, which rely on ICMP messages.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4821 describes how a sender can discover the largest packet size a network path can carry. It tests larger packets and observes whether they arrive, reducing dependence on ICMP warnings.

subtitle: A packet-size discovery method that tests the path instead of relying only on ICMP messages.

tldr.problem: Traditional Path MTU Discovery can fail when ICMP Packet Too Big messages do not reach the sender, leaving connections unable to make progress.
tldr.mechanism: A packetization layer sends larger probe packets and uses acknowledgements and loss reports to learn which sizes the path carries. An isolated lost probe can indicate an MTU limit rather than congestion.
tldr.outcome: The method can supplement classical discovery or operate without ICMP. RFC 4821 has been updated by RFC 8899.

today: RFC 4821 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8899.

sections.title: Why Probe the Path
sections.content:
Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (PLPMTUD) extends the IPv4 and IPv6 discovery methods in RFC 1191 and RFC 1981. Those methods rely on ICMP Packet Too Big messages. If such a message is lost or not processed, a connection can hang.

PLPMTUD starts with packets expected to work and probes with progressively larger packets. It runs mainly in the transport layer, such as TCP, or another layer that chooses packet boundaries. It does not require cooperation from the remote peer.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender can test packet sizes directly instead of depending only on network warning messages. It begins with a size that works and then tests larger packets.

sections.title: Requirements for Reliable Probing
sections.content:
Links must consistently discard packets larger than their MTU. A packetization layer using PLPMTUD must have a timely and accurate way to learn which packets were lost. Normal congestion control remains active except when only an isolated probe is lost; in that case, the layer should suppress the normal congestion reduction and limit how often it does so.

When the MTU rises, congestion state must be rescaled so the byte window or data rate does not increase as a side effect. Implementations must also let applications send packets larger than the current effective PMTU, but smaller than the first-hop link MTU, for probing and diagnosis.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender must be able to tell whether a test packet was lost. It treats one lost test differently from losses that also affect ordinary traffic.

sections.title: Sharing Path Information Across Layers
sections.content:
PLPMTUD splits work between the IP layer and the packetization layer. IP is a suitable place to keep shared path information, collect ICMP messages, track IP header sizes, and manage MTU information from interfaces. The packetization layer handles probes and verification because those procedures depend on data recovery and congestion control.

A probe's final size must include IP headers and any other headers between IP and the packetization layer. An implementation may represent a path by its destination address, but should store the minimum PMTU when middleboxes can expose different path sizes at the same address. Network or subnet numbers must not be used as the path representation.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP layer can keep MTU information that several connections share. Each data protocol still needs to create probes and measure their results.

sections.title: Searching for a Packet Size
sections.content:
The method tracks search_low, search_high, and eff_pmtu. The lower value represents a size the network is expected to carry; the upper value is a probe size expected to be too large; the effective PMTU is the largest non-probe packet permitted for that flow. A probe must be larger than search_low and no larger than search_high.

A successful probe raises the known lower bound. The RFC recommends starting search_low at a conservative size and gives 1024 bytes as a likely safe example; 1400 bytes is described as a possible initial effective PMTU compromise. Once the search converges, a timer restarts it later; that timer must be at least 5 minutes, with 10 minutes recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a size known to work and a size that may be too large. Each successful or failed test narrows the range between them.

sections.title: Interpreting Probe Results and Timeouts
sections.content:
If a probe is acknowledged, the path carried a packet of that size, so PLPMTUD raises its lower bound and may raise the effective PMTU. If only the probe is lost, the layer treats that as evidence that the probe exceeded the path MTU and lowers its upper bound. It should not treat that isolated loss as congestion.

If the probe and other packets are lost, the result is inconclusive: the state does not change, and the same size can be tried after recovery. A full-stop timeout can indicate an ICMP black hole or a network change; after repeated timeouts, the method reduces its estimates. Implementations should also verify a raised MTU by checking whether the packet loss rate increases.
sections.plainLanguage: A successful test confirms that its size can pass. If other traffic is lost at the same time, the sender cannot tell whether size or congestion caused the failure.

sections.title: TCP, SCTP, and Security Considerations
sections.content:
TCP creates probes by sending an oversized segment containing data; a failed probe can require retransmission. SCTP can use a padding chunk attached to a minimum-length HEARTBEAT. Datagram protocols that rely on IP fragmentation need an additional probing protocol, while an application can probe with an echo and padding mechanism.

The RFC says PLPMTUD is at least as secure as the standard IPv4 and IPv6 discovery methods. An implementation can ignore ICMP, but an attacker could still reduce performance by causing probe packets to be lost. A packetization protocol that is not trusted should not be allowed to change shared path state.
sections.plainLanguage: Different protocols create test packets in different ways. A program that shares MTU information should only let trusted protocols change it.
